questions.title: Why does the Fifth Circuit review sufficiency of an indictment de novo rather than on a different standard of review?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the opinion and I see that the court states it 'reviews the sufficiency of an indictment de novo' under United States v. Rafoi. But I thought most appeals standards might be 'clearly erroneous' or 'clearly settled law.' Is de novo the correct standard for sufficiency of indictment in general, or is there something specific about how the Fifth Circuit interprets 18 U.S.C. 1348 that requires this heightened review?

questions.title: How is the 'pump and dump' scheme in United States v. Constantinescu distinguishable from the right-to-control theory rejected in Ciminelli?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued that because they only deprived the victims of economic information, the case should fall under the *Ciminelli* right-to-control theory. Since the Supreme Court said *Ciminelli* only depends on information deprivation, why does the Fifth Circuit suggest this particular 'pump and dump' case isn't a right-to-control issue? I don't see how simply posting false info ensures the view that the victims part with property.

questions.title: Under the Kousisis decision, does the government still need to prove the victim suffered a net pecuniary loss to establish fraud intent?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the paragraph where the court discusses Kousisis. It says that a defendant violates fraud statutes regardless of whether the victim 'sought to leave the victim economically worse off.' So if the investors in the pump scheme actually gained money from the following stocks, does that mean they still satisfy the intent to defraud element, or else does Kousisis abolish the need to show any deprivation of money by the victim?

questions.title: What are the three specific purposes an indictment must fulfill according to the language used in United States v. Gaytan, and how do they relate to Double Jeopardy?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions the garlic test from United States v. Gaytan: (1) enumerate elements, (2) inform defendant, (3) provide double jeopardy defense. I understand the legal theory here, but can you break down exactly how the third element—double jeopardy—works procedurally. Does the court check if the indictment itself, rather than the prosecution's future conduct, protects against double jeopardy?

questions.title: How does the court determine that the 'inducement to purchase securities' satisfies the §1348 requirement to deprive a victim of 'money or property'?
questions.question_body: The opinion says securities fraud statutes protect 'money or property' but the district court thought 'economic information' wasn't enough. The court says the indictment alleges the defendants 'fradulently induced their followers to purchase securities' so they gained property. But if the prompt doesn't allege the investor actually *lost* that property, why does the court say the intent to defraud their followers of money is sufficient even if the transaction itself sees the victim gaining the securities back in exchange?
